Bias records systematic displacement from a target, while variance records sampling spread. **Mean squared error** (MSE) combines them:

$$
\operatorname{MSE}(T;\theta)=\mathbb{E}[(T-\theta)^2].
$$

Squaring does two jobs: it prevents positive and negative errors from canceling, and it penalizes large errors more heavily than small ones. Because the error is measured in milliseconds here, MSE is measured in squared milliseconds. Its square root returns to the response unit, but the decomposition below is naturally expressed on the squared scale.

We first derive the bias-variance decomposition, then compare two estimators across empirical speaker resamples, and finally use that comparison to show why lower bias need not imply lower mean squared error.

## The decomposition

Add and subtract $\mathbb{E}[T]$ inside the square:

$$
T-\theta=(T-\mathbb{E}[T])+(\mathbb{E}[T]-\theta).
$$

Expanding and taking expectations gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{MSE}(T;\theta)
&=\mathbb{E}[(T-\mathbb{E}[T])^2]
+2\mathbb{E}[T-\mathbb{E}[T]](\mathbb{E}[T]-\theta)
+(\mathbb{E}[T]-\theta)^2\\
&=\operatorname{Var}[T]+\operatorname{Bias}(T;\theta)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The cross-term vanishes because $\mathbb{E}[T-\mathbb{E}[T]]=0$.

## Comparing two estimators by nonparametric bootstrap

The target remains the empirical mean /I/ duration among the observed adult women. The resampling unit is a speaker row, and both estimators use the observed group size.

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-mse
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
x <- subset(vowels, speaker_type == "woman" & vowel == "I")$duration_ms
theta <- mean(x)
n <- length(x)

set.seed(20261019)
replicates <- 20000L
draws <- replicate(replicates, sample(x, n, replace = TRUE), simplify = FALSE)
estimates <- list(
  `Sample mean` = vapply(draws, mean, numeric(1)),
  `Sample median` = vapply(draws, median, numeric(1))
)

mse_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(estimates), function(name) {
  value <- estimates[[name]]
  bias <- mean(value) - theta
  variance <- mean((value - mean(value))^2)
  mse <- mean((value - theta)^2)
  data.frame(estimator = name, variance_ms2 = variance,
             squared_bias_ms2 = bias^2, mse_ms2 = mse)
}))

stopifnot(max(abs(
  mse_table$mse_ms2 - mse_table$variance_ms2 - mse_table$squared_bias_ms2
)) < 1e-8)
mse_table
```

Each row of `mse_table` verifies the identity numerically: `variance_ms2 + squared_bias_ms2` equals `mse_ms2`. The column names retain the squared unit so that a student does not mistake MSE for a typical millisecond error.

The sample mean has MSE `r sprintf("%.3f", mse_table$mse_ms2[mse_table$estimator == "Sample mean"])` ms(^2), whereas the sample median has MSE `r sprintf("%.3f", mse_table$mse_ms2[mse_table$estimator == "Sample median"])` ms(^2) for this mean target.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-mse
#| fig-cap: "Variance and squared-bias components of MSE for estimating the empirical mean."
mse_components <- rbind(
  data.frame(estimator = mse_table$estimator,
             component = "Sampling variance", value_ms2 = mse_table$variance_ms2),
  data.frame(estimator = mse_table$estimator,
             component = "Squared bias", value_ms2 = mse_table$squared_bias_ms2)
)

ggplot(mse_components, aes(estimator, value_ms2, fill = component)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Sampling variance" = "grey55",
                               "Squared bias" = "#8B1A1A")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = expression("Mean squared error (ms"^2*")"), fill = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

This comparison is conditional on the empirical target and the observed Hillenbrand cohort. It does not imply that mean duration is always the scientifically appropriate target, nor that the sample median is generally inferior.

## Recap and forward link

1. MSE averages squared error relative to a named target.
2. It decomposes into sampling variance plus squared bias because the centered cross-term has expectation zero.
3. A biased estimator may have lower MSE if its reduction in variance is large enough.

The [confidence-interval page](confidence-intervals.qmd) next studies procedures that attach a range to each estimate.

## Check your understanding

1. Why does the cross-term disappear in the MSE derivation?
2. Which component accounts for most of the sample median's MSE here?
3. Could a biased estimator have lower MSE than an unbiased estimator?
4. Why must an MSE comparison name its target?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The cross-term contains $\mathbb{E}[T-\mathbb{E}[T]]$, which equals zero. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Squared bias accounts for slightly more of the sample median's MSE here than sampling variance does. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Yes. A biased estimator can have lower MSE than an unbiased estimator when its variance reduction exceeds its squared bias. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Both bias and squared error are defined relative to a target; changing the target can change the estimator ranking. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
